newsitem.title: FRANCE: French rugby match offer election glimpse.
newsitem.headline: French rugby match offer election glimpse.

text.p: A rugby match on Saturday embodies the choice French President Jacques Chirac has given voters by calling a snap parliamentary election -- and the uncertainty about what his own future will be made of.

As the French ponder their left-right choice in Sunday's election runoff, Chirac will sit in the official stand for the French Rugby Union final with the leaders of the two camps: Socialist Lionel Jospin and Gaullist Philippe Seguin.

If the right recovers from its first-round defeat to retain power, Chirac will reap the fruits of his snap election gamble with a smooth passage through the five remaining years of his seven-year term.

If Jospin's Socialist-Communist-Greens alliance confirms its stunning first-round upset, the Gaullist president faces being a lame duck in a "cohabitation" with a hostile government bent on overturning his austerity policies geared to fulfilling the criteria for the European single currency.
Seguin, the likely prime minister if the right wins, warned voters that "cohabitation" would be as tough as a rugby match.

"Cohabitation is...institutionalised division. It is a Chirac-Jospin match. Every day. A pretty prospect that we must imperatively avoid," he said, urging voters not to bring back leftists "ghost of the past" who held power for a decade and were routed in 1993.
"I ask French men and women...to confirm and amplify the first-round vote," an increasingly confident Jospin, 59, said.

He said that Chirac had asked voters to speak their mind and must accept the verdict. If the left won, he would have to share power with a left-wing government to the end of his term in 2002 rather than call another snap election in a year as he is entitled to.

Unpopular Prime Minister Alain Juppe, who took the blame for the first-round fiasco and has vowed to quit whatever the runoff result, voiced confidence in his last campaign rally in his hometown of Bordeaux. "We will and we must win," he said.
But the right clearly sounded on the defensive as the left started talking about cabinet line-ups and government moves.
The conservatives appealed to voters not to let "the trap slam shut" and think of the future rather than venting short-term irritation at record unemployment and austerity.

After Jospin said a French left-wing win would stun and cheer Europe after Labour's victory in Britain, Seguin said that electing a Socialist-Communist alliance would only stun Russia and eastern Europe which had got rid of communism.

Communist leader Robert Hue spelled out his terms for joining a possible Socialist-led government, including pay rises and new taxes on investment earnings, anathema to the ruling centre-right. Jospin aides said he would reject any condition.
The two allies have bickered over European monetary union, which the Communists oppose but the Socialists generally favour.

Jospin has set conditions for joining the euro, including relaxing the Maastricht criteria and gearing the single currency towards creating jobs. He advocates boosting the consumers' purchasing power in order to boost economic growth.
Despite his fierce condemnation of the left, Seguin also advocates making jobs the priority and says budget cuts to fulfill the Maastricht criteria must not be so harsh as to paralyse growth.

Saying he had understood the voters' first round warning, Chirac dumped Juppe and entrusted the campaign leadership to the socially-minded Seguin and ultra-liberal ex-finance minister Alain Madelin, a duo the left has derided as unworkable.

The last stretch of the campaign was marred by violence as two people, including a Socialist parliamentary candidate, were injured in a clash between anti-racist militants and supporters of Jean-Marie Le Pen far-right National Front in the poor Paris suburb of Mantes-la-Jolie.

A local government spokeman said Le Pen had thrown to the ground the Socialist candidate and town mayor Anette Pleuvast-Bergeal. Le Pen, a 68-year-old former paratrooper, said he was suing the spokesman for slander and admitted he had "slightly pushed" some people who blocked his way.
